newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl sends message to critics, Paris on EMU target.
newsitem.headline: Kohl sends message to critics, Paris on EMU target.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl has moved to silence critics within his coalition and send a signal to the new French government by vowing that Germany will meet a key target for joining the single European currency, financial analysts said on Tuesday.

But they said Kohl had little chance of honouring his promise to cut the state deficit to 3.0 percent of German gross domestic product, the most troublesome target for economic and monetary union (EMU).
"We're staying with 3.0 -- that's no problem -- and with the schedule," Kohl said on Tuesday. "That stands, it is binding, there is no use discussing it any more."

His comments contrasted with an admission last week by Dominique Strauss-Kahn, finance minister in the Socialist-led French government, that Paris could not meet the target this year, when countries will be judged for the planned launch of the euro in 1999.
German analysts said Kohl's long-awaited declaration was designed primarily to take the wind out of the sails of Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber.

Stoiber has led the attack on any attempt to soften the EMU criteria from his position as a leading member of the Christian Social Union, the Bavarian sister party of Kohl's Christian Democratic Union.

"Kohl clearly wanted to put an end to the whole damaging debate," said Ralf Kugelstadt, economist at UBS Global Research in Frankfurt. "It was threatening to cause divisions in the coalition and he wanted to get the debate out of the headlines."
Sources close to the Bundesbank said Kohl was also offering a veiled hint to Paris that Bonn would not tolerate any massive overrun of the deficit target.
"I would interpret these statements to mean that Germany has absolutely no interest in beginning a currency union with partners whose deficits are quite a bit higher," the official said.
"Budget deficits of 3.6 or 3.8 percent would definitely be too much for Germany."
Kohl's long-held insistence that the EMU launch could not be delayed had played into the hands of Stoiber, who has tirelessly said the emphasis should be on the criteria and not the timing.
Sepaking at a Munich business conference attended by Stoiber, Kohl said parliament had given its word it would agree to the euro only if the criteria were met.
Kohl had long avoided mentioning the 3.0 percent deficit target but he was forced by Stoiber's persistent fear-mongering to renew the old promise.

"Kohl wanted to take the wind out of Stoiber's sails," said Ruetger Teuscher, an economist at DB Research in Frankfurt. "Kohl knows that a discussion about delaying the euro is fraught with considerable risk and it was hurting his government."
With opinion polls showing most Germans oppose the euro replacing their cherished marks, Stoiber has been playing to public fears about the dangers of a weak euro.
"Germans are very sensitive about the issue," said Rudolf Zwiener, economist at DIW research institute in Berlin. "But it is unrealistic to think Germany will reach the 3.0 percent target."
Zwiener and many other analysts believe Germany's deficit will be about 3.2 to 3.5 percent of GDP in 1997.

"This was purely a political manoeuvre by Kohl to keep the euro on track," said Bernd Kruth, economist at Westdeutsche Landesbank in Duesseldorf. "Some day Kohl is going to end up saying 'sorry, we didn't reach the 3.0 percent target'."
Alison Cotrell, an economist at PaineWebber International in London, said Kohl had been put in "an impossible position by Stoiber and the French government".
Kohl would have somehow to build a bridge between the 3.0 percent deficit pledge to Stoiber and the new French government's admission it will not meet the target.
Most analysts see little point of launching an EMU without both Germany and France taking part.

"Kohl has painted himself into a corner ...He is caught between the Munich and Paris governments," she said. "The best he can hope for is the dispute will only simmer and not boil over. He has to tell Stoiber what he wants to hear and avoid mentioning the fact that France will not adhere to the deficit targets."
